rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting the risk of incomplete elution. The retention window will guide narrower, faster gradients in subsequent injections.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF. Shortening the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed tests whether full resolution can be retained with a faster last-peak time.

The critical pair responds strongly to gradient slope, losing resolution at 6 minutes. Test the intermediate 8-minute gradient to recover full resolution while shortening the method relative to injection 1.
Test whether higher temperature improves the critical pair’s selectivity enough to permit the faster 6-minute gradient. Injection 3 remains a fully resolved, maximum-CRF fallback.

Raise the starting organic fraction and narrow the window while keeping the slope close to the successful 8-minute gradient. This tests a shorter separation without the selectivity losses observed at 60 C.
Test an intermediate temperature to improve the critical pair’s selectivity and shorten retention. At 50 C, the other pairs may retain sufficient separation without the near-coelution seen at 60 C.

Shift the starting fraction upward and trim the endpoint while preserving approximately the successful gradient slope. This should shorten retention while testing whether the early and critical pairs remain fully resolved.

Reduce the gradient slope one grid step to lift the marginal R = 1.46 pair above 1.5. The last peak previously eluted near 0.51 organic fraction, so an endpoint of 0.60 should still keep all peaks within the gradient.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while making the gradient slightly shallower to support the critical pair. This also tests how much the early pair can be compressed before losing full resolution.

With a maximum-CRF method secured, test a much steeper gradient for a faster separation on the other side of a possible critical-pair elution-order reversal. This exploratory run will show whether strong compression creates a second fully resolved operating window.

Test whether lowering temperature separates the critical pair in the steep-gradient regime. Holding the gradient fixed isolates temperature selectivity and checks whether the late pair remains adequately resolved.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at low temperature to alter the critical pair’s selectivity while preserving some early retention. The narrower, steep gradient explores a faster operating window beyond the near-coelution region.

Return to the fastest fully resolved window and make the gradient slightly shallower to strengthen its marginal critical-pair resolution. This tests a more robust maximum-CRF method with only a small expected increase in last-peak time.

Test whether lower temperature preserves early-pair separation at a higher starting organic fraction. The shallower gradient is intended to compensate for the critical pair’s loss of resolution as the starting fraction rises.

Measure temperature selectivity locally around the fastest fully resolved method, changing only temperature from injection 9. The early pair should gain separation; the critical pair will determine whether cooler operation offers useful resolution margin.

Use the 6-minute grid to obtain a slope between injections 7 and 8, targeting just enough critical-pair resolution without the slower retention of injection 8. The lower starting fraction also provides more early-pair separation than injection 9.

Test whether a 5 C increase lifts injection 7’s marginal critical pair above R = 1.5 while shortening retention. The early pair is the main risk, so this run checks the upper temperature boundary for the faster window.

Test a shallower gradient and modestly higher temperature than injection 14 to recover critical-pair resolution at the higher starting fraction. This explores whether that window can fully resolve the mixture while retaining adequate early-pair separation.

Refine injection 9 by lowering the endpoint one step to strengthen its marginal critical-pair resolution. This targets a compact maximum-CRF method with more resolution margin, rather than sacrificing separation for further speed.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a nearby method for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak well below 10 minutes. Lower temperature should separate the early pair, while the shallower gradient should strengthen the critical middle pair.

Lower the starting fraction relative to injection 17 while preserving its gradient slope, aiming to recover early-pair resolution at 55 C. This tests whether higher-temperature operation can retain full resolution with a short gradient.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 9 using the 6-minute grid, seeking a shorter last-peak time while retaining maximum CRF. The critical pair’s previous R = 1.58 leaves only a small margin, making this a focused speed-boundary test.

Back off from the speed boundary and test a more balanced resolution margin: cooling injection 19 should improve its limiting early pair, while the shallower slope should keep the middle pair resolved. Maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 9 remaining the fastest fully resolved result.

Preserve injection 19’s successful slope through the critical middle pair, then switch to a hold using a 2-minute gradient. This tests whether the late compounds can elute promptly at 0.40 organic while retaining full resolution and maximum CRF.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 20 to shorten retention while using its critical-pair resolution margin. This final refinement targets maximum CRF with stronger early-pair separation than the 50 C methods; injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved result.
